title: Demonstrate an understanding of ethics and traditions pertaining to the hunting of wild animals

lessons.title: Best practice, the law and respect for others
lessons.html:
Ethical hunting starts with the law

Ethics is about doing what is right even when nobody is watching. For a professional hunter, the minimum standard is the law: provincial hunting permits and seasons, TOPS regulations for listed species, the Firearms Control Act 60 of 2000, and the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 where it applies. Generally accepted best practice goes further than the law.

Best practices

  • Hunt only with valid permits and on properties where hunting is allowed.
  • Use a rifle and bullet suitable for the species, and make sure you and your client can shoot accurately at the distance.
  • Take only shots that give a high chance of a quick, clean kill: a standing animal, broadside or quartering, within range, with a clear view of the vital area.
  • Follow up every wounded animal until it is found, no matter how long it takes.
  • Use the whole animal where possible: venison, skins and by-products.
  • Select old, mature males past their breeding prime where trophies are sought.
  • Keep accurate hunting registers.

Respect for the rights of others

  • Landowners: get permission, follow farm rules, close gates, do not hunt outside agreed areas.
  • Neighbours: never shoot across fences or near boundaries, and do not cross fences after a wounded animal without permission.
  • Farm workers and communities: tell them where and when you are hunting so they are safe.
  • Clients: honest descriptions of what animals are available, fair prices, no false promises.
  • Other hunters and the public: be discreet. Do not post graphic pictures that disrespect the animal.
  • Cultural respect: some communities have traditional beliefs about certain animals and places; respect them.

lessons.title: Fair chase and hunting traditions
lessons.html:
The principle of fair chase

Fair chase means hunting a wild animal in a way that does not give the hunter an unfair or improper advantage, and gives the animal a reasonable chance to escape. It is the heart of ethical hunting.

Fair chase in practice

  • The animal must be free-ranging within an area large enough for it to evade the hunter.
  • Do not shoot animals from vehicles, at night with spotlights, or in small enclosures unless a legal management cull requires it.
  • Do not chase animals with vehicles or aircraft to tire them before the hunt.
  • Do not shoot animals that are drugged, trapped, recently released from a crate, or helpless in water or a fence.
  • Do not use baits or calls where the law or the hunt rules forbid them.

"Canned" hunting, where a captive-bred animal is released into a small area to be shot, is widely condemned and in many cases illegal. A professional hunter who takes part damages the reputation of the whole industry.

Hunting traditions and history

Hunting in southern Africa is ancient. San hunter-gatherers tracked game for thousands of years with bows, poisoned arrows and remarkable tracking skills, many of which are still used by trackers today. Many African cultures had rules about which animals could be hunted, by whom and when. Colonial-era hunting in the 1800s greatly reduced game numbers, leading to the creation of reserves such as the Sabie Game Reserve, which later became the Kruger National Park. In the late twentieth century, private game ranching grew rapidly, and today hunting contributes to conservation by giving wildlife a value that encourages landowners to keep land under natural veld.

Traditions to keep

  • Respect the animal after the shot: a moment of silence, the "last bite" tradition in some hunting cultures.
  • Thank the tracker and skinners and share the success.
  • Pass on skills and ethics to young hunters.

Key points

  • The law is the minimum; best practice goes further.
  • Take only shots that give a quick, clean kill, and always follow up wounded animals.
  • Respect landowners, neighbours, workers, clients and communities.
  • Fair chase gives the animal a reasonable chance to escape; canned hunting is unethical.
  • Hunting has deep roots, from San trackers to modern game ranching.
